title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: Levin had noticed long ago that when people make you uncomfortable by being excessively pliant and meek, you very soon find them unbearable for being touchy and irritable. He felt this was how things would go with his brother. And in fact Nikolay's gentleness did not hold up long. The very next morning he turned irritable and seemed bent on picking fights with his brother, going after him on his tenderest points.

Levin felt to blame and couldn't put things right. He felt that if they had both dropped the pretense and spoken — as the saying goes — from the heart, meaning if they had said only what they were actually thinking and feeling, they would simply have looked into each other's faces, and Konstantin could only have said, "You're dying, you're dying!" and Nikolay could only have answered, "I know I'm dying, but I'm afraid, I'm afraid, I'm afraid!" And nothing more could have been said, if they were saying only what was in their hearts. But life like that was impossible, and so Konstantin tried to do what he had been trying to do all his life and never could learn — what so many people, as far as he could see, knew how to do so well, and without which there was no living at all. He tried to say what he wasn't thinking, and felt all the while that it rang false, that his brother caught him at it and was exasperated.
On the third day Nikolay drew his brother into explaining his scheme again, and began not just attacking it but deliberately confounding it with communism.
"You've simply borrowed an idea that isn't yours, and you've distorted it, and you're trying to apply it where it doesn't apply."

"But I'm telling you, it has nothing to do with it. They deny the justice of property, of capital, of inheritance, while I don't deny this chief stimulus." (Levin felt disgusted with himself for using such expressions, but ever since he had been absorbed in his work, he had unconsciously been reaching more and more often for foreign, un-Russian words.) "All I want is to regulate labor."
"Which means you've borrowed an idea, stripped it of everything that gave it any force, and want to pass it off as something new," Nikolay said, tugging angrily at his necktie.
"But my idea has nothing in common...."

"At least that idea," said Nikolay Levin, with an ironical smile, his eyes flashing maliciously, "has the charm of — what shall I call it? — geometrical symmetry, of clearness, of definiteness. It may be a Utopia. But once you grant the possibility of making a _tabula rasa_ of the entire past — no property, no family — then labor would organize itself. But you gain nothing...."
"Why do you mix things up? I've never been a communist."
"But I have been, and I think it's premature but rational, and that it has a future, just like Christianity in its first centuries."
"All I'm maintaining is that the labor force ought to be investigated from the point of view of natural science — that is, studied, its qualities ascertained...."

"But that's a complete waste of time. That force finds its own form of activity according to the stage of its development. There were slaves first, everywhere; then sharecroppers; and now we have the half-crop system, rent, and day laborers. What are you trying to find?"

Levin suddenly lost his temper at this, because at the bottom of his heart he was afraid it was true — true that he was trying to hold the balance between communism and the familiar forms, and that this was barely possible.
"I'm trying to find a way of working productively, for myself and for the laborers. I want to organize...." he answered heatedly.
"You don't want to organize anything; you just want, the way you've always wanted, to be original — to pose as someone who doesn't simply exploit the peasants but has an idea behind it."
"All right, that's what you think — now leave me alone!" Levin answered, feeling the muscles of his left cheek twitch uncontrollably.
"You've never had convictions, and you don't have any now; you only want to flatter your vanity."
"Fine, then; leave me alone!"
"And I will leave you alone! and it's high time I did, and to the devil with you, and I'm sorry I ever came!"
Despite all Levin's efforts to calm his brother afterward, Nikolay would hear none of it, insisting it was better to part — and Konstantin saw it was simply that life had become unbearable to him.
Nikolay was just getting ready to go when Konstantin went in to him again and asked him, rather unnaturally, to forgive him if he had hurt his feelings in any way.
"Ah, magnanimity!" said Nikolay, and he smiled. "If you want to be right, I can give you that satisfaction. You're right; but I'm going all the same."
Only at the very moment of parting did Nikolay kiss him, and looking suddenly, strangely, and seriously at his brother, he said:

"Anyway, don't think badly of me, Kostya!" — and his voice quivered. Those were the only words spoken sincerely between them. Levin knew they meant, "You see, you know, that I'm in a bad way, and perhaps we shall not see each other again." Levin knew it, and the tears poured from his eyes. He kissed his brother once more, but he couldn't speak, and didn't know what to say.
Three days after his brother's departure, Levin too set off on his foreign tour. Running into Shtcherbatsky, Kitty's cousin, on the train, Levin astonished him by his depression.
"What's the matter with you?" Shtcherbatsky asked him.
"Oh, nothing; there isn't much happiness in life."
"Not much? Come with me to Paris instead of Mulhausen. I'll show you how to be happy."
"No, I'm done with all that. It's time I was dead."
"Now there's a good one!" Shtcherbatsky said, laughing. "Why, I'm only just getting ready to begin."
"Yes, I thought the same not long ago — but now I know I'll soon be dead."

Levin was saying what he had honestly been thinking lately. He saw nothing but death, or the approach toward death, in everything. But his cherished scheme only absorbed him the more. Life had to be got through somehow until death came. Darkness had fallen over everything for him; but precisely because of this darkness he felt that the one guiding thread in it was his work, and he gripped it and clung to it with all his strength.
